title: Ottoman Anatolia
subtitle: 1500–1800 · The Kızılbaş, the Celali Revolts, the Provincial Notables and the Ports of the Levant

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The conquest of the East, the princes' provinces, the Celali captains and the notable houses of the eighteenth century

entries.group: The Conquest and the Classical Provinces
entries.label: The princes' provinces
entries.hint: Sultans' sons were sent as governors with their households to the sanjaks of Amasya, Manisa, Konya, Kütahya and Trabzon to learn government, and made provincial courts there of poets and artists. Selim I, Süleyman and Mehmed III were governors. After the death of Murad III in 1595 the sons were kept at Istanbul instead, which ended the practice.
entries.note: Leslie Peirce, The Imperial Harem (1993); Metin Kunt, The Sultan's Servants (1983).

entries.group: The Conquest and the Classical Provinces
entries.label: Selim I and the conquest of the East
entries.hint: Selim, governor of Trabzon and a rebel against his father, took the throne in 1512, crushed the Kızılbaş and the Safavid shah at Çaldıran in 1514, ended the Dulkadir emirate in 1515 and, with the Kurdish scholar Idris Bitlisi, brought the Kurdish emirates of the southeast into the empire as hereditary sanjaks. He then took Syria and Egypt.
entries.note: Idris Bitlisi, Selim Shah-nama; Celalzade Mustafa; Colin Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650 (2002).

entries.group: The Conquest and the Classical Provinces
entries.label: The provinces of the classical empire
entries.hint: Anatolia was divided in the sixteenth century into the beylerbeyliks of Anadolu, Karaman, Rum (Sivas), Zülkadriye, Diyarbekir and Erzurum, each divided into sanjaks under a sanjak bey with a force of timar-holding cavalry. The system was the heart of the Ottoman army and the model of the empire's government.
entries.note: Halil İnalcık, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age (1973); Suraiya Faroqhi, Approaching Ottoman History (1999).

entries.label: Karayazıcı, Deli Hasan and the Celali captains
entries.hint: Karayazıcı Abdülhalim, a former clerk, led thousands of discharged soldiers and peasants in revolt in 1598, defeating the governors' forces and the sultan's troops and holding much of central Anatolia, with his brother Deli Hasan and, later, Canbulatoğlu Ali Pasha in Syria and Kalenderoğlu. The name 'Celali' became a general term for rebels.
entries.note: Mustafa Akdağ, Celali isyanlarında Büyük Kaçgunluk (1963); William Griswold, The Great Anatolian Rebellion (1983).

entries.label: The ayan houses
entries.hint: By the eighteenth century many districts of Anatolia were held by local notable families — the Karaosmanoğlu of Manisa, the Çapanoğlu of Yozgat, the Cebbarzade of Adana and Canikli Hacı Ali Pasha of Trabzon — who acted as tax-farmers, militia commanders and quasi-hereditary governors, in the name of the sultan. They are the great-power men of the age.
entries.note: Yuzo Nagata, Tarihte ayanlar (1997); Faroqhi, The Ottoman Empire and the World Around It (2004).
keywords: Canikli Hacı Ali Pasha of Trabzon

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Şahkulu's revolt, Çaldıran, the Celali rebellions, Abaza Mehmed Pasha and the Safavid wars

entries.label: Şahkulu's rebellion
entries.hint: In April 1511 a Safavid preacher called Şahkulu, 'the slave of the Shah', raised the Turkmen of the Teke region in revolt against Bayezid II, killed the grand vizier Hadım Ali Pasha in the battle that broke the army sent against him, and marched on Bursa before being killed. The rebels' ranks moved towards the Safavid cause.
entries.note: Celalzade; Hoca Saadeddin; Ahmet Yaşar Ocak, Alevi and Bektaşi Inanışlarının İslam Öncesi Temelleri (1983).

entries.label: Selim's suppression of the Kızılbaş
entries.hint: Selim, before leaving for Çaldıran, had the Kızılbaş sympathisers of the eastern provinces listed and, according to later sources, up to 40,000 of them killed or imprisoned. The fatwa of the scholars had declared them apostates. The campaign marked the Alevi communities for centuries as a suspect minority.
entries.note: Celalzade; Ocak 1983; Rıza Yıldırım, Turkmens between two Empires (2008).

entries.label: Çaldıran
entries.hint: Selim's army, with its artillery and janissary muskets, broke the Safavid cavalry of Shah Ismail at Çaldıran on the Azerbaijan frontier, took his capital Tabriz for a few days and returned to winter in Amasya. The Shah's belief in his own invincibility was shattered. The battle fixed the Ottoman–Safavid frontier at the east end of Anatolia.
entries.note: Idris Bitlisi; Celalzade; Rudi Matthee on the Safavid wars.

entries.label: The Treaty of Amasya and the later wars
entries.hint: The Peace of Amasya of 1555, the first formal treaty between the Ottomans and the Safavids, ended a long war and set the frontier through the Caucasus and Iraq. Wars broke out again in 1578 and 1603; Murad IV took Baghdad in 1638 and the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 fixed a border that has hardly changed since. Anatolia was the staging area for all of them.
entries.note: Treaty of Amasya (1555); Treaty of Zuhab (1639); Rudi Matthee, Persia in Crisis (2012).

entries.label: The Celali rebellions
entries.hint: For a decade, bands of unemployed students of the madrasas (suhte), discharged musketeers (sekban) and peasants fought the imperial troops across Anatolia, defeated pashas, took towns and sacked Kütahya. The grand vizier Kuyucu Murad Pasha put them down in 1607–1610 with great massacres. Villages emptied in the 'Great Flight' to the cities.
entries.note: Akdağ 1963; Griswold 1983; Karen Barkey, Bandits and Bureaucrats (1994).

entries.label: Sekban and levend bands
entries.hint: Musketeer mercenaries (sekban), hired by the state and by the pashas and discharged after campaigns, formed armed bands that lived off the countryside and joined the notables' retinues. The sekban and the levend became a permanent social element which governors had to feed or fight.
entries.note: Barkey 1994; Faroqhi 2004; Metin Kunt 1983.

entries.label: Abaza Mehmed Pasha's revolt
entries.hint: Abaza Mehmed Pasha, governor of Erzurum, rose in 1622 to avenge the murder of the young sultan Osman II by the janissaries, took much of eastern Anatolia and besieged Ankara and the road to Istanbul, and was only reconciled in 1628. His rising shows the force of provincial governors.
entries.note: Naima; Evliya Çelebi, Seyahatname 2; Barkey 1994.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The cadastral surveys, the kadi courts, the malikâne, the deportations and the settlement of the tribes

entries.label: The cadastral surveys
entries.hint: In each reign from Selim I to Murad III the state made detailed surveys of villages, households, fields and revenue, tahrir defterleri, to assign timars and tax. They list every village by name, with its taxpayers and their dues. They are the main source for the population and economy of sixteenth-century Anatolia, which, they show, grew rapidly.
entries.note: Ömer Lütfi Barkan, 'Essai sur les données statistiques des registres de recensement' (1957); Heath Lowry; Faroqhi 1999.

entries.label: The kadi courts and their registers
entries.hint: The kadi, the judge of each district, kept registers (sicil) of the cases heard, sales, loans, wills, and the sultan's orders and prices, in which people of all ranks appear. The Kayseri registers from the 1580s and those of Bursa, Konya, Ankara and Trabzon are the richest social source for early modern Anatolia.
entries.note: Ronald Jennings, 'Kadi, court and legal procedure in 17th c. Ottoman Kayseri' (1978); Haim Gerber, State, Society and Law in Islam (1994).

entries.label: The sürgün to Cyprus
entries.hint: After the conquest of Cyprus in 1571 the government ordered families of farmers and artisans from the Anatolian districts, among them Karaman, Içel and Aydın, to be moved to the island, a thousand households at a time, and ordered the local officials to carry out the move. The deportations were part of a policy of settling frontier lands.
entries.note: Mühimme defterleri (Ottoman imperial orders), 1570s; Halil İnalcık, 'Ottoman methods of conquest' (1954).

entries.label: The tribal settlement at Raqqa
entries.hint: In 1691 the state ordered Turkmen and Kurdish tribes of the Anatolian plateau and the Syrian steppe to be settled around Raqqa on the Euphrates, to halt their raiding and to secure the frontier. The effort failed within a few years. It was one of many attempts to settle the nomads.
entries.note: Reşat Kasaba, A Moveable Empire (2009); Orhan Sakin on the Raqqa settlement.

entries.label: The malikâne and tax-farming
entries.hint: In 1695 the state began selling tax revenues for life (malikâne) to the highest bidders, instead of annual tax farms, to raise cash in a long war. The holders subcontracted them to local notables, who consolidated property and power in the provinces. It is the legal basis of the rise of the ayans.
entries.note: Mehmet Genç, 'Osmanlı maliyesinde malikâne sistemi' (1975); Ariel Salzmann, 'An ancien régime revisited' (1993).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Kızılbaş and Alevi communities, Pir Sultan Abdal, the Bektashis, the Karamanlides and Sabbatai Zevi

entries.label: The Kızılbaş and the Alevi communities
entries.hint: In the villages of the Anatolian east and centre, Turkmen and Kurdish communities which had followed the Safavid shaykhs kept their own religion with a devotion to Ali and the Twelve Imams, hereditary holy lineages (ocak) and rituals led by dedes. After Çaldıran the state treated them as a heresy, and they withdrew into remote villages. They became known as Alevis.
entries.note: Ocak 1983; Irène Mélikoff, Hadji Bektach (1998); Markus Dressler, Writing Religion (2013).

entries.label: The Bektashi order's second founder
entries.hint: Balım Sultan, appointed head of the Bektashi lodge at Hacıbektaş in about 1501, gave the order an organisation, rules of celibate and married dervishes and a more orthodox cast. The order became the spiritual home of the janissary corps. He is called the Second Master.
entries.note: Bektashi tradition (Velayetname); John Kingsley Birge, The Bektashi Order of Dervishes (1937).

entries.label: Pir Sultan Abdal
entries.hint: Pir Sultan Abdal, a poet and Alevi saint of the Banaz village near Sivas, wrote songs of devotion to Ali and protest against injustice in a simple Turkish syllabic verse, and is said to have been hanged at Sivas for revolt against the governor. He is the most beloved of the Alevi poets.
entries.note: Pir Sultan Abdal, Deyişler; Sabri Dede; Abdülbaki Gölpınarlı and Pertev Naili Boratav, Pir Sultan Abdal (1943).

entries.label: The Karamanlides
entries.hint: The Orthodox Christians of Cappadocia and Karaman, who spoke Turkish and not Greek, wrote and printed Turkish in Greek letters (Karamanlıca), with prayers, catechisms and Gospels. The first books were printed in Europe in the eighteenth century. They are a unique example of a Christian community which kept its religion while changing its language.
entries.note: Evangelos Balta, Karamanlidika (1987); Richard Clogg, 'The Greek millet in the Ottoman Empire'.

entries.label: Sabbatai Zevi at Smyrna
entries.hint: In 1665 Nathan of Gaza proclaimed Sabbatai Zevi of Smyrna, a Kabbalist, to be the Messiah, and Jewish communities from Amsterdam to Persia were swept by hopes of redemption. He was arrested by the Ottomans in 1666 and converted to Islam at Adrianople. A part of his followers, the dönme, remained.
entries.note: Gershom Scholem, Sabbatai Sevi (1973); Cengiz Şişman, The Burden of Silence (2015).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Iznik tiles, the Uşak carpet, the poems of Karacaoğlan and the palace at Doğubayazıt

entries.label: The tiles of Iznik
entries.hint: In the town of Iznik potters made a fritware with a white body and brilliant underglaze painting in cobalt, turquoise, green and a raised red, first in blue-and-white and then with tulips, carnations and saz leaves, for dishes, lamps and the tiles of the sultans' mosques. The works declined after 1700; Kütahya took over.
entries.note: Nurhan Atasoy and Julian Raby, Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey (1989).

entries.label: The carpets of Uşak
entries.hint: Weavers in the villages of the Uşak region in west Anatolia wove wool carpets with large medallions, in a type known in Europe as Holbein and Lotto carpets after the painters who depicted them. They were exported to Italy, Flanders and England as luxury goods. They are among the glories of Ottoman art.
entries.note: Walter Denny, The Origins of Oriental Carpets; Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts, Istanbul.

entries.label: The âşık and the saz
entries.hint: The âşıks, minstrels who accompanied their poems on the long-necked lute (saz or bağlama), were performers at weddings, coffee houses and festivals, and used the form of the deyiş and a contest of improvised verse. They were the keepers of an oral literature of Anatolia's Turkmen, Alevi and Sufi communities.
entries.note: Evliya Çelebi, Seyahatname; Pertev Naili Boratav, Halk Edebiyatı Dersleri.

entries.label: Karacaoğlan
entries.hint: Karacaoğlan, a wandering minstrel of the Turkmen of the Taurus, sang of love, nature and the nomad's life in the language of the people, in a Turkish syllabic verse. Some hundreds of his songs have been passed down and he is regarded as one of the finest of the folk poets.
entries.note: Karacaoğlan, Şiirleri (ed. Sadettin Nüzhet Ergun, 1948).

entries.label: The palace at Doğubayazıt
entries.hint: The İshak Pasha Palace, begun in 1685 by Çolak Abdi Pasha, a Kurdish chieftain, and finished in 1784 by his grandson İshak Pasha, on a ledge beneath Mount Ararat, is a complex of courts, mosque, harem and tombs with a mixture of Ottoman, Seljuk, Persian, Armenian and Georgian elements. It stands for the power of a provincial dynasty.
entries.note: İshak Pasha Palace inscriptions; Godfrey Goodwin, A History of Ottoman Architecture (1971).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Evliya Çelebi, Katib Çelebi and Niyazi-i Mısri

entries.label: Evliya Çelebi's travel book
entries.hint: Evliya Çelebi travelled for forty years through the empire and beyond it and recorded in ten volumes of the Seyahatname the towns, monuments, customs, language and lore of every region, with long accounts of Anatolian cities and their notables, tales of heroes and miracles. It is a unique source and a masterpiece of Ottoman prose.
entries.note: Evliya Çelebi, Seyahatname (ed. Dankoff et al., 1996–2007); Robert Dankoff, An Ottoman Mentality (2004).

entries.label: Niyazi-i Mısri
entries.hint: Niyazi-i Mısri, a Sufi poet from Malatya, wrote Turkish and Arabic poetry of the unity of being in the tradition of Ibn Arabi, with a following in Anatolia, and founded a branch of the Khalwati order. He was banished several times, to Rhodes and Lemnos, and died in exile.
entries.note: Niyazi-i Mısri, Divan; Barbara von Schlegell; Ahmed Yaşar Ocak.

entries.label: Katib Çelebi's Cihannüma
entries.hint: Katib Çelebi, a civil servant and scholar, wrote the Cihannüma, a geography of the world, drawing on Ptolemy, Islamic geographers and the new European atlases of Mercator and Blaeu, with a long description of Anatolia's provinces and roads. It was printed in Istanbul in 1732 by Ibrahim Müteferrika.
entries.note: Katib Çelebi, Cihannüma (1732 print); Orhan Şaik Gökyay; Gottfried Hagen, Ein osmanischer Geograph (2003).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The silk of Bursa, Ankara's mohair, the rise of Izmir and the new crops

entries.label: The silk of Bursa
entries.hint: Bursa, with its silk markets and its weavers, was the centre of the Ottoman silk trade, buying Persian raw silk and local cocoons and making brocades, velvets and kemha for the court and export. The wars with Persia, and Venice's competition, made the trade fluctuate. It was among the great manufacturing towns.
entries.note: Halil İnalcık, 'Bursa and the commerce of the Levant'; Suraiya Faroqhi 1984; Bursa kadi registers.

entries.label: Angora wool and Ankara's mohair
entries.hint: The long silky hair of the Angora goat of the Ankara region was spun and woven into a fine cloth called sof (mohair), which was exported with its yarn to France, England and the Netherlands. The craft of sof weaving was a mainstay of Ankara's economy, and the export of yarn formed a part of Ankara's links to European markets.
entries.note: Suraiya Faroqhi, Towns and Townsmen of Ottoman Anatolia (1984); Edhem Eldem, French Trade in Istanbul.

entries.label: The rise of Izmir
entries.hint: Smyrna, a small town at the end of the sixteenth century, became in the seventeenth the leading port of the eastern Mediterranean, exporting silk, cotton, mohair, figs, raisins and carpets and taking in European cloth. English, French, Dutch and Venetian merchants had consuls and quarters, and the city had Greek, Armenian and Jewish communities as large as its Muslim one.
entries.note: Daniel Goffman, Izmir and the Levantine World (1990); Elena Frangakis-Syrett, The Commerce of Smyrna (1992).

entries.label: The new crops
entries.loc: Black Sea coast and the Aegean
entries.hint: Maize came to the Black Sea valleys and the Aegean in the seventeenth century, tobacco to the coasts and cotton to the plains of the Çukurova and the Aegean, as cash crops for the new European markets. The crops and the new patterns of farming changed rural Anatolia.
entries.note: Faroqhi 2004; Şevket Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire (2000).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The musket, the menzil roads and Sinan's bridges

entries.label: The menzil road system
entries.hint: The post-road from Istanbul to Baghdad, with stations (menzil) at a day's ride apart, had horses for imperial couriers and rooms for officials, supplied by the surrounding villages. Many caravanserais, bridges and fountains were built by the state, pashas and pious donors. It was the backbone of the provincial empire.
entries.note: Colin Heywood on the menzil; Halil Sahillioğlu; Faroqhi 2004.

entries.label: Firearms in the countryside
entries.hint: As the state shifted from cavalry to musketeers, large numbers of Anatolian peasants and townsmen were armed, hired as sekban and discharged, and brought their muskets home. Firearms, once a monopoly of the janissaries, were widely in private hands and made the Celali revolts possible. The military revolution had social effects.
entries.note: Gábor Ágoston, Guns for the Sultan (2005); Griswold 1983; Barkey 1994.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Levant Company at Izmir, the Armenian caravans and the Safavid frontier

entries.label: The Safavid frontier and its marches
entries.hint: The Kurdish emirates and Turkmen tribes of the marches held the frontier between the two empires for the Ottomans, paid tribute, supplied troops and traded with both sides. Their loyalty depended on the terms offered. The Ottoman frontier policy rested on these chiefs.
entries.note: Evliya Çelebi; Şerefname of Sharaf Khan Bidlisi (1597); Martin van Bruinessen, Agha, Shaikh and State (1992).

entries.label: The Levant Company and the consuls
entries.hint: The capitulations of France (1569) and England (1580) allowed merchants of those nations to trade at Smyrna and the Anatolian ports under their own law, with consuls. The English Levant Company had its factors there. The agreements gave Western merchants a position that was later the basis of European penetration.
entries.note: Capitulations (France 1569; England 1580); A. C. Wood, A History of the Levant Company (1935); Goffman 1990.

entries.label: The Armenian caravans
entries.hint: Armenian merchants, above all of New Julfa near Isfahan, carried Persian silk to Anatolia and the European ports. Their caravans crossed Erzurum, Tokat and Bursa and reached Izmir and Aleppo, with branch houses in the Mediterranean and beyond. It was the largest merchant network of the empire.
entries.note: Sebouh Aslanian, From the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean (2011); Ina Baghdiantz McCabe, The Shah's Silk for Europe's Silver (1999).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Little Ice Age, the pressure of numbers and the long decentralisation

entries.label: Population pressure and the suhte
entries.hint: The population of Anatolia grew rapidly through the sixteenth century, and land became short. Large numbers of unemployed young men — the madrasa students, suhte, and the levend — wandered and were hired by pashas. The pressure underlies the Celali revolts, and the history of the next century.
entries.note: Barkan 1957; Mustafa Akdağ, Türkiye'nin iktisadi ve içtimai tarihi (1959); Griswold 1983.

entries.label: The Little Ice Age and the famine
entries.hint: Years of cold and drought in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, recorded in tree rings and in chronicles, reduced the harvests of the plateau and the pastures of the nomads and brought dearth, with the Celali revolts. The Great Flight of the villagers from the land has been connected to this climate.
entries.note: Sam White, The Climate of Rebellion in the Early Modern Ottoman Empire (2011).

entries.label: The age of the notables
entries.hint: By the eighteenth century, as the central state lost its grip, the wealth and power of the provinces passed to the ayans, who held districts almost as principalities, and provided troops to the sultan and kept order. The province was ruled in practice by local houses until the reforms of Mahmud II.
entries.note: Yuzo Nagata 1997; Faroqhi 2004; Kasaba 2009.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Women in the kadi's court, the slaves of the Black Sea and the Jews of Izmir

entries.label: The slaves of the Black Sea road
entries.hint: Through the ports of Trabzon, Samsun and Sinop came slaves from the Caucasus, the Crimea and the steppe, sold in the markets of Anatolia and Istanbul. In the eastern Mediterranean ports captured Europeans were sold or ransomed. Enslaved men and women worked in households, in the fields and in the armies of the pashas.
entries.note: Halil İnalcık, 'The Black Sea slave trade'; Ehud Toledano, The Ottoman Slave Trade and Its Suppression (1982); Alan Fisher.

entries.label: The Jews of Izmir
entries.hint: Izmir's Jewish community, which grew with Sephardic refugees of the 1490s and merchants from the Mediterranean, was by the seventeenth century the largest in Anatolia, with a rabbinical school and trade in textiles, figs and silk. It was the home of Sabbatai Zevi.
entries.note: Jacob Barnai, The Jews in the Ottoman Empire; Goffman 1990.

entries.label: Women in the kadi's court
entries.hint: The kadi registers show women of every class as parties to sales, loans, inheritance cases, waqf foundations and suits for divorce, and in some places a third of the cases are brought by women. They were not hidden in the home. Women took their disputes with their husbands, families and neighbours to court.
entries.note: Ronald Jennings, 'Women in early 17th century Ottoman judicial records' (1975); Haim Gerber 1994; Leslie Peirce, Morality Tales (2003).
